content: The second edition of the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment was developed in alignment with the requirements of the WHO Guideline Review Committee. The Guideline Development Groups (GDGs) evaluated the certainty of the most recent evidence regarding the effectiveness and potential harms of interventions, as well as evidence on values, preferences, equity, resource use, acceptability, and feasibility of implementation. These considerations were used to update or formulate recommendations and determine their strength. The GDGs assessed the implications of the best available evidence for each population subgroup at risk, including the likelihood of progression from TB infection to active TB disease and the incidence of TB disease in these groups compared to the general population. The guiding principle was that individual benefit should outweigh risk when recommending testing for TB infection (TBI) and TB preventive treatment (TPT). Testing for TBI is preferred when feasible to identify individuals at the highest risk of developing TB. Tools such as chest radiography with computer-aided detection (CAD) software, C-reactive protein (CRP) testing, and WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostic tests (mWRD) should be used to rule out active TB disease before initiating TPT. The need for additional resources to implement the guidelines should not be seen as a barrier but rather as an opportunity to mobilize appropriate funding levels for programmatic implementation. This edition includes 21 recommendations covering critical steps in the programmatic management of TPT (PMTPT) and the cascade of preventive care. These steps include identifying at-risk populations (e.g., people with HIV, household contacts, and others), screening for and ruling out TB disease, testing for TBI, providing treatment and support, managing adverse drug reactions, and monitoring adherence and treatment completion. Most recommendations from the 2020 guidelines remain unchanged. However, new updates include the addition of a six-month daily levofloxacin regimen (6Lfx) as a TPT option for individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in all settings, subject to specific conditions. Recommendations from other WHO guidelines relevant to PMTPT published since 2020 are also incorporated. Operational challenges requiring urgent action by countries to meet global targets are highlighted. The updated guidelines are accompanied by the second edition of the WHO operational handbook on TB preventive treatment, which provides practical details for programmatic implementation. Both publications are part of a six-module series of WHO consolidated guidelines and operational handbooks addressing all aspects of TB prevention and care. The guidelines emphasize identifying populations at increased risk of TB progression, such as people with HIV, household contacts of TB patients, and other high-risk groups. For example, adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB disease based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART), pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of their level of immunosuppression or availability of TBI testing. Infants under 12 months living with HIV who have been in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have active TB disease should also receive TPT. Similarly, children aged 12 months or older living with HIV in high TB transmission settings should be offered TPT as part of comprehensive HIV prevention and care, regardless of TB contact history. Children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may also receive TPT. Household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB, regardless of HIV status, are another priority group. Children under five years of age who are household contacts and are found not to have active TB disease should receive TPT, even if TBI testing is unavailable. Older children, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts may also be considered for TPT based on clinical evaluation and national guidelines. Other high-risk groups include individuals initiating anti-tumor necrosis factor treatment, those receiving dialysis, individuals preparing for organ or hematological transplants, and those with silicosis. These groups should be systematically tested and treated for TBI. Systematic testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. Screening for TB disease is essential before initiating TPT. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, current cough, or a history of TB contact should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing these symptoms. If active TB disease is excluded, they should be offered TPT regardless of age. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB disease. However, individuals reporting any of these symptoms should be further evaluated for TB and other diseases and offered TPT if active TB is excluded. Chest X-rays, CRP testing, and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests may also be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. Among HIV-negative household contacts aged five years or older and other risk groups, the absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings may be used to rule out TB disease before initiating TPT. Testing for TBI can be performed using either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBST) may also be used as an alternative. Recommended TPT regimens include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternative regimens include a one-month daily rifapentine plus isoniazid regimen or four months of daily rifampicin. For individuals exposed to MDR/RR-TB, six months of daily levofloxacin is recommended as a TPT option. TB infection (TBI) is defined as a state of persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically manifest TB disease. Approximately one-fourth of the global population is estimated to be infected with M. tuberculosis. While most individuals with TBI are asymptomatic and non-infectious, they remain at risk of developing active TB disease, particularly within the first five years after initial infection. The risk of progression to active TB disease is influenced by several factors, with immunological status being the most significant. The WHO End TB Strategy emphasizes TPT as a critical component of efforts to eliminate TB. The efficacy of currently available TPT regimens ranges from 60% to 90%. However, the potential benefits of treatment must be carefully weighed against the risk of drug-related adverse events. Mass population-wide testing and treatment for TBI are not currently feasible due to imperfect tests, the risk of serious adverse drug reactions, and high costs. Instead, TPT should be targeted to high-risk groups where the benefits outweigh the risks. The updated guidelines aim to expand TPT coverage, including for individuals exposed to MDR/RR-TB, while addressing operational challenges to achieve global targets. The guidelines are intended for use by national TB and HIV programs, policymakers, clinicians, and other stakeholders involved in TB prevention and care.
